title: The Story of an Hour
attribution: The Story of an Hour by Kate Chopin (1894). Public domain. One hyphenation artifact ("fellow- creature") in the source transcription has been corrected to "fellow-creature".
body: Knowing that Mrs. Mallard was afflicted with a heart trouble, great care was taken to break to her as gently as possible the news of her husband’s death.

It was her sister Josephine who told her, in broken sentences; veiled hints that revealed in half concealing. Her husband’s friend Richards was there, too, near her. It was he who had been in the newspaper office when intelligence of the railroad disaster was received, with Brently Mallard’s name leading the list of “killed.” He had only taken the time to assure himself of its truth by a second telegram, and had hastened to forestall any less careful, less tender friend in bearing the sad message.

She did not hear the story as many women have heard the same, with a paralyzed inability to accept its significance. She wept at once, with sudden, wild abandonment, in her sister’s arms. When the storm of grief had spent itself she went away to her room alone. She would have no one follow her.
There stood, facing the open window, a comfortable, roomy armchair. Into this she sank, pressed down by a physical exhaustion that haunted her body and seemed to reach into her soul.

She could see in the open square before her house the tops of trees that were all aquiver with the new spring life. The delicious breath of rain was in the air. In the street below a peddler was crying his wares. The notes of a distant song which some one was singing reached her faintly, and countless sparrows were twittering in the eaves.
There were patches of blue sky showing here and there through the clouds that had met and piled one above the other in the west facing her window.

She sat with her head thrown back upon the cushion of the chair, quite motionless, except when a sob came up into her throat and shook her, as a child who has cried itself to sleep continues to sob in its dreams.

She was young, with a fair, calm face, whose lines bespoke repression and even a certain strength. But now there was a dull stare in her eyes, whose gaze was fixed away off yonder on one of those patches of blue sky. It was not a glance of reflection, but rather indicated a suspension of intelligent thought.

There was something coming to her and she was waiting for it, fearfully. What was it? She did not know; it was too subtle and elusive to name. But she felt it, creeping out of the sky, reaching toward her through the sounds, the scents, the color that filled the air.

Now her bosom rose and fell tumultuously. She was beginning to recognize this thing that was approaching to possess her, and she was striving to beat it back with her will—as powerless as her two white slender hands would have been.

When she abandoned herself a little whispered word escaped her slightly parted lips. She said it over and over under her breath: “free, free, free!” The vacant stare and the look of terror that had followed it went from her eyes. They stayed keen and bright. Her pulses beat fast, and the coursing blood warmed and relaxed every inch of her body.
She did not stop to ask if it were or were not a monstrous joy that held her. A clear and exalted perception enabled her to dismiss the suggestion as trivial.

She knew that she would weep again when she saw the kind, tender hands folded in death; the face that had never looked save with love upon her, fixed and gray and dead. But she saw beyond that bitter moment a long procession of years to come that would belong to her absolutely. And she opened and spread her arms out to them in welcome.

There would be no one to live for her during those coming years; she would live for herself. There would be no powerful will bending hers in that blind persistence with which men and women believe they have a right to impose a private will upon a fellow-creature. A kind intention or a cruel intention made the act seem no less a crime as she looked upon it in that brief moment of illumination.

And yet she had loved him—sometimes. Often she had not. What did it matter! What could love, the unsolved mystery, count for in face of this possession of self-assertion which she suddenly recognized as the strongest impulse of her being!
“Free! Body and soul free!” she kept whispering.

Josephine was kneeling before the closed door with her lips to the keyhole, imploring for admission. “Louise, open the door! I beg; open the door—you will make yourself ill. What are you doing, Louise? For heaven’s sake open the door.”
“Go away. I am not making myself ill.” No; she was drinking in a very elixir of life through that open window.

Her fancy was running riot along those days ahead of her. Spring days, and summer days, and all sorts of days that would be her own. She breathed a quick prayer that life might be long. It was only yesterday she had thought with a shudder that life might be long.

She arose at length and opened the door to her sister’s importunities. There was a feverish triumph in her eyes, and she carried herself unwittingly like a goddess of Victory. She clasped her sister’s waist, and together they descended the stairs. Richards stood waiting for them at the bottom.

Some one was opening the front door with a latchkey. It was Brently Mallard who entered, a little travel-stained, composedly carrying his grip-sack and umbrella. He had been far from the scene of accident, and did not even know there had been one. He stood amazed at Josephine’s piercing cry; at Richards’ quick motion to screen him from the view of his wife.
But Richards was too late.
When the doctors came they said she had died of heart disease—of joy that kills.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, who first told Mrs. Mallard the news of her husband's death?
options: Her sister Josephine
Her husband's friend Richards
A newspaper reporter
Her husband himself

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how did Mrs. Mallard first react to the news of her husband's death?
options: She wept at once, with sudden, wild abandonment
She refused to believe it
She fainted immediately
She calmly asked for details

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does Mrs. Mallard go to her room and ask that no one follow her?
options: She wants to hide the fact that she is not upset
She wants to be alone with the powerful feeling that is beginning to overtake her
She wants to pack her belongings and leave town
She is angry at her sister for telling her the news

questions.prompt: What does the word Mrs. Mallard keeps whispering, "free," reveal about her true feelings?
options: She is in complete denial that he has died
She believes he is still alive somewhere
Beneath her grief, part of her feels a sense of liberation
She is practicing what she will say at the funeral

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does Mrs. Mallard mean by her reflection on imposing "a private will upon a fellow-creature"?
options: She believes her husband committed an actual legal crime
She feels that anyone imposing their will on another is wrong, even when well-meant
She thinks Josephine's kindness was really a hidden cruelty
She is condemning the railroad company for the accident

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the central irony of the passage?
options: The doctors correctly diagnose the cause of her death
Her husband is revealed to have caused the railroad accident himself
The doctors believe joy killed her, but it was really the loss of her newfound freedom
Josephine is blamed for causing her sister's death

questions.prompt: According to the passage, who walks through the front door near the end of the story?
options: Richards, her husband's friend
A doctor
Brently Mallard, her husband
A telegram messenger

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does Richards try to screen Brently Mallard from his wife's view?
options: To prevent her from divorcing her husband
To protect her from the shock of the sudden, unexpected sight of her husband
To keep the two men from fighting
To hide that Brently was involved in the accident

questions.prompt: Which best states the overall theme suggested by the passage?
options: True love always triumphs over personal ambition
The desire for personal freedom can be stronger than love or grief
Grief is best processed alone rather than with family
Railroad travel was dangerous in the era of the story

questions.prompt: In the passage, what does "importunities" mean, as in "she arose at length and opened the door to her sister's importunities"?
options: Persistent requests or pleading
Silent stares
Angry accusations
Written letters

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what news arrived about the railroad, and whose name was on the list of the dead?
options: A shipwreck, with Richards' name among the missing
A railroad disaster, with Brently Mallard's name among those killed
A fire, with Josephine's name among the injured
A robbery, with no casualties reported

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what could Mrs. Mallard see and hear through the open window?
options: A funeral procession passing by
Trees stirring with new spring life, and a peddler crying his wares below
Snow falling over a quiet street
Fireworks over the town square

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does Mrs. Mallard's dull, unfocused stare suggest about her state of mind just after the news?
options: She has fallen asleep in the chair
She is not yet consciously processing the powerful feeling approaching her
She is carefully planning her husband's funeral
She is physically blind from crying

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what is suggested by Mrs. Mallard's thought that she would "live for herself" in the years to come?
options: She anticipates a new independence now that her husband is gone
She plans to move away and cut off contact with her sister
She intends to remarry immediately
She fears she will be lonely without anyone to care for her

questions.prompt: Which best describes the shift in Mrs. Mallard's feelings over the course of the passage?
options: She moves from anger at her husband to forgiveness
She moves from shock and grief toward a secret, growing sense of freedom
She moves from disbelief to acceptance of a lie
She moves from fear of her sister to trust in her sister

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why is Richards described as "too late" when Brently Mallard enters?
options: He arrived after the ambulance had already left
He could not prevent Mrs. Mallard from seeing her husband before the shock hit her
He missed the chance to buy tickets for the same train
He failed to send the telegram in time

questions.prompt: In the passage, what does it mean that Mrs. Mallard "was drinking in a very elixir of life through that open window"?
options: She was literally drinking a medicinal tonic
She was watching children drink from a fountain
She was feeling a powerful surge of vitality and possibility
She was remembering a childhood memory of the window
